title: Subqueries
summary: A subquery is a query inside another query. Its answer helps the outer query do its job.
introduction: A subquery is a query inside another query. Its answer helps the outer query do its job. First find an average. Then use that answer to find rows above the average. Read the inner question before the outer one.
learningObjectives: Use a scalar subquery as a value in WHERE
Filter with IN, NOT IN and EXISTS subqueries
Write correlated subqueries and derived tables
Structure multi-step queries with common table expressions

blocks.text: A subquery that returns exactly one row and one column can be used wherever a single value can. The database evaluates the inner query first (the average price is about 26.12) and then runs the outer query with that value:

blocks.content:
name                | price
--------------------+------
Mechanical keyboard | 89
Monitor stand       | 39.5

blocks.text: When the inner query returns a list of values, `IN` tests membership. This finds the customers who have never bought electronics by listing those who have and excluding them:

blocks.code:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (
  SELECT o.customer_id
  FROM orders o
  JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
  WHERE p.category = 'Electronics'
);

blocks.title: NOT IN and NULL
blocks.text: If the subquery can return a NULL (for example from a nullable `customer_id`), `NOT IN` returns no rows at all, because `x <> NULL` is never true. Add `WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL` to the subquery or use `NOT EXISTS`, which does not have the problem. A second trap: a scalar subquery that returns several rows raises an error in PostgreSQL and MySQL, while SQLite silently uses the first row.

A *correlated* subquery refers to the outer row (`p.id` below) and is evaluated once per outer row. `EXISTS` is true when the subquery returns at least one row; `NOT EXISTS` is the robust way to express "has no such row". Products never ordered in a quantity above one:
A correlated subquery can also appear in the SELECT list, producing one computed value per row:

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.id;

blocks.content:
name              | orders
------------------+-------
Ada Lovelace      | 2
Grace Hopper      | 2
Linus Torvalds    | 2
Margaret Hamilton | 1
Guido van Rossum  | 1

blocks.text: Correlated subqueries are easy to read but can be slow on large tables because they run once per row; a join with GROUP BY often does the same work in one pass.
A subquery in the FROM clause acts as a temporary table and needs an alias. It is the natural way to aggregate an already computed value, such as the average value of an order line:

Deep nesting gets hard to read. A **common table expression** (CTE) names a subquery up front with `WITH name AS (...)` and lets the main query use it like a table, even several times. SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL 8+, SQL Server and Oracle all support it. Customers who spent more than the average customer:

blocks.code:
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(p.price * o.quantity) AS spent
  FROM orders o
  JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, ROUND(t.spent, 2) AS spent
FROM totals t
JOIN customers c ON c.id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.spent > (SELECT AVG(spent) FROM totals)
ORDER BY spent DESC;

blocks.content:
name             | spent
-----------------+------
Ada Lovelace     | 102.5
Guido van Rossum | 89

blocks.text: `totals` is used twice: as a table in the join and inside the scalar subquery that computes the average. Recursive CTEs (`WITH RECURSIVE`) extend the idea to hierarchical data such as org charts and category trees.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Find the products that cost less than the cheapest electronics product, then rewrite the query with a CTE named `cheapest`.

blocks.title: Try it yourself

questions.question: What does `WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)` compare each price against?
questions.explanation: The inner query is independent of the outer row, so it is computed once and yields a single number that every row is compared with.

questions.question: `NOT EXISTS` behaves correctly even when the subquery's columns contain NULL values.
questions.explanation: EXISTS only asks whether any row comes back, so NULLs inside those rows do not matter. NOT IN is the construct that breaks with NULLs.

seo.title: SQL Subqueries – IN, EXISTS, Derived Tables and WITH
seo.description: Learn SQL subqueries: scalar subqueries, IN and NOT IN, correlated subqueries with EXISTS, derived tables in FROM, and common table expressions with WITH.
